summary: Specifies a MIB module for managing multicast over UNI 3.0 and 3.1 ATM networks. It lets network management tools monitor the multicast address resolution parts of ATM. It is a proposed standard and replaces RFC 2366.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a list of dials and gauges for checking on multicast traffic in an old type of network called ATM, so people can watch it from a management tool.

subtitle: A management database module for watching and configuring IP multicast over ATM through SNMP.

tldr.problem: IP multicast over ATM networks relies on a Multicast Address Resolution Server (MARS), its clients and optional multicast servers. Operators need a standard way to look at and manage them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the IPATM-IPMC-MIB module in three groups, for MARS clients, MARS servers and MARS multicast servers (MCS). Each group is a set of tables of settings, virtual circuits, group address blocks and counters.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2366, which carried a clerical error in its module number assignment. It is written for UNI 3.0 and 3.1 based ATM.

today: RFC 2417 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2366. The IANA note says RFC 2366 assigned the module number wrongly through a clerical error, and the module was re-rooted from snmpModules to mib-2. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The SNMP Framework Behind the MIB
sections.content:
This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for network management protocols. It is written in a form compatible with the SNMPv2 SMI and semantically identical to the peer SNMPv1 definitions.

The RFC lists the parts of the SNMP Network Management Framework it relies on: the SMI (RFC 1902), the Textual Conventions (RFC 1903), the Conformance Statements (RFC 1904), SNMP itself (STD 15, RFC 1157), the Protocol Operations (RFC 1905) and MIB-II (STD 17, RFC 1213). Objects are defined with a subset of ASN.1, and each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is a big agreed list of things a manager is allowed to look at on a machine. Everyone uses the same list so the manager's tools work on every machine.

sections.title: Terms Borrowed From MARS
sections.content:
The MIB manages the entities described in RFC 2022, which defines multicast support over UNI 3.0/3.1 ATM. An understanding of that document is assumed. The RFC recaps five terms.

  • A multicast group is a set of endpoints where a packet sent by one is received by all the others.
  • A Multicast Address Resolution Server (MARS) distributes group membership information to endpoints.
  • A client or endpoint is an ATM-attached host or router registered with a MARS. It may open ATM Virtual Channels (VCs) to other members or use a multicast server.
  • A cluster is the set of clients managed by a MARS.
  • A Multicast Server (MCS) sets up VCs between endpoints in a group and forwards their data traffic on their behalf.
sections.plainLanguage: A MARS is like a class register that says who belongs to which club. A club's members can call each other directly, or send everything through one helper who repeats it to everybody.

sections.title: Three Groups of Tables
sections.content:
The MIB is meant for a system where one or more MARS clients, MARS servers or MARS multicast servers are running. It splits into three major groups under the module marsMIB, assigned as mib-2 57.

The client group has five tables: client, client multicast group, client backup MARS, client VC and client statistics. The server group has eight: MARS, multicast group, VC, registered client, registered multicast server, statistics, host map and server map. The multicast server group has five, mirroring the client group: MCS, MCS multicast group, MCS backup MARS, MCS VC and MCS statistics.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one binder of gauges for the people in the clubs, one for the register keeper and one for the helper who repeats announcements.

sections.title: What the Client Tables Record
sections.content:
The client table has one row per MARS client and is indexed by ipAdEntAddr and marsClientIndex, which ties it to the ipAddrTable of RFC 1213. A row holds the client's ATM address, the ATM address of its default MARS, its 32-bit Host Sequence Number, its 16-bit cluster member identifier and its default MTU, which defaults to 9180 bytes.

It also holds many timers and retry limits. For example, the failure timer defaults to 10 seconds, the join/leave retransmit limit has a maximum of 5, and the idle timer for new VCs has a recommended default of 20 minutes. The registration object takes five values, shown below.

Other tables list the IP multicast address blocks a client uses, its backup MARS entries, its open VCs and its counters. A block is a minimum and maximum group address, and when they are equal the block is a single group.
sections.plainLanguage: Each client has a card listing its own address, its helper's address, how long to wait before giving up and how many times to retry. Other cards list its clubs and its open phone lines.

sections.title: Server and Multicast Server Objects
sections.content:
The MARS server table describes a MARS with its ATM address, status and timers. Its multicast group table lists address blocks, and each block's usage is hostMap (1), serverMap (2) or hostServerMap (3), meaning it is used in the host map table, the server map table or both.

The host map and server map tables record the mappings the MARS maintains between multicast groups and clients, and between groups and MCSs. Registered client and registered multicast server tables list who has registered. The multicast server group repeats the client pattern for an MCS, with its own address, default MARS, registration state, VCs and counters.
sections.plainLanguage: The register keeper's binder also has lists showing which clubs are served by direct calls and which by the helper.

sections.title: The Fault Notification
sections.content: The module defines one notification, marsFaultTrap. The text says it is sent to the manager whenever a fault condition occurs on a MARS, and it carries the MARS address and the server status object, marsAddr and marsServStatus.
sections.plainLanguage: If the register keeper has trouble, an alarm bell rings in the control room and tells the manager which keeper it is.

sections.title: Conformance Groups
sections.content: Conformance is defined separately for clients, servers and multicast servers. Each has a module compliance statement and an object group, so a system that runs only one role can claim compliance for that role. The compliance statements relax a number of objects to read-only. Many of the object write-access entries read 'Write access is not required.'
sections.plainLanguage: A club member only needs the club member's gauges, and the keeper only needs the keeper's gauges. Many of the dials can be look-only.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Several objects have a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create. These may be sensitive, and allowing SET operations in a non-secure environment can harm network operations. SNMPv1 alone is such an environment, and even a secure network such as one using IPSec does not control who on it may SET the objects.

The RFC recommends the SNMPv3 security features, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 2274) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2275). It also notes that read access may need access control too.
sections.plainLanguage: If anyone could turn the dials, they could break the system. So only trusted people should get a key, and sometimes even looking should need one.
